title: moe-coldstart-burst-recovery-long-context-behavior
content:
Summary

This note captures a focused investigation into cold-start and burst-recovery behavior for mixture-of-experts (MoE) models when serving mixed-length workloads (short chat + occasional long-context documents) across Llama-like, Mistral, and Qwen architectures. The guiding question: why do MoE endpoints exhibit intermittent multi-100ms latency spikes for the first few tokens after idle periods or sudden sequence-length increases, and which mitigations provide the best cost/latency tradeoffs without materially increasing steady-state cost?

Motivation & context

We observed customer reports and internal alerts showing recurring P95/P99 spikes on MoE-backed routes that otherwise have good steady-state throughput. Spikes often align with: (a) an idle window (endpoint receives no traffic for tens of seconds), (b) sudden multi-turn long-context requests (context length jumps from <64 to >2048 tokens), or (c) short bursty traffic after autoscaler downscales. Existing remediation (keepwarm traffic) reduces but does not eliminate spikes and increases billable tokens. This doc documents experiments across models, the measured failure modes, and prototype mitigations.

Experimental setup

- Hardware: 1x A100-80GB (single-GPU experiments) and 4x H100-80GB (multi-GPU endpoint sharded tests).
- Serving stack: Redwood inference runtime (stable-2025-06), custom MoE expert allocator from experiments branch.
- Models: Llama-2-MoE-30B (FP16), Mistral-MoE-32B (bfloat16), Qwen-MoE-14B (FP16). We used quantized variants only in a later sweep.
- Workloads: short-chat baseline (avg seq=32 tokens), long-doc injection (single request with seq=4096 tokens), burst arrival patterns: single request, 10 req/s for 3s, then idle 120s.
- Metrics: token-latency (per-token wall time), first-token latency, P50/P95/P99, GPU utilization, host->device memcpy time, routing CPU time (gating + top-k selection), memory consumption (total VRAM), and expert activation counts.

Findings

1) Two distinct cold penalties
- Warmup cold penalty: first-token latency after idle is dominated by kernel launch and expert KV cache cold misses. Measured first-token spikes of ~140—260 ms on A100 for MoE models; warmed steady-state per-token was 12—20 ms for same models. Llama/Mistral showed similar patterns but Qwen-MoE had slightly higher gating overhead (~20% worse first-token).
- Context-scaling cold penalty: when a request jumps to long context (e.g., from 32->4096), we see additional pause (~90—180 ms) at the point where existing KV cache needs to expand / prefetch for longer autoregressive steps. This appears even when endpoint has recent traffic.

2) Bottleneck decomposition for first-token spike (typical numbers on A100):
- Host->Device memcpy for initial KV stash: 25—45 ms
- Gating/top-k selection on CPU (per-token batch size 1): 18—35 ms (Python->C++ overhead included)
- Kernel launch / small-kernel inefficiency: 30—70 ms
- Expert activation synchronization and memcpy for activated experts: 40—110 ms
Note: wall-time includes overlap; peaks sum to observed 140—260 ms.

3) Expert sparsity and fragmentation effects
- Endpoints with higher expert fanout (top-2 gating) activate more experts and incur more memcpy overhead; top-1 gating has smaller cold overhead but worse quality tradeoffs in some cases.
- Fragmentation: if previous traffic touched a disjoint set of experts than the next long request requires, the system experiences near-full rehydrate cost. In practice, 60% of observed spikes correlate with expert set mismatch.

4) Quantization interaction
- Int8/4-bit quantized expert kernels reduce steady-state runtime but increase cold-start memcpy volume (compressed representations still require format conversion on-device), increasing first-token penalty by ~10—25 ms in our tests.

Mitigations evaluated (and results)

A) Lightweight keepwarm (low-rate synthetic tokens)
- Approach: random 1 token requests every 10s routed to route-specific warm handler; cheap but billable.
- Result: reduces first-token spike magnitude by ~45% and reduces frequency by ~60% but increases baseline cost by ~3–6% depending on traffic.

B) Eager gating precompute (server-side only)
- Approach: when endpoint is idle, run a tiny gating-only step (no expert execution) that warms gating state and records most-likely experts for typical prefixes. When a request arrives, route immediately to precomputed expert allocations.
- Result: eliminated ~30% of the memcpy cost (experts pre-allocated) and reduced first-token latency by ~35% with negligible extra token billing (gating-only ops counted as lightweight internal ops). Implementation complexity: low latency but requires caching of gating fingerprints per route and lifecycle management.

C) Staggered expert keepwarm (budgeted expert warming)
- Approach: for each endpoint keep a rotating small set of experts resident (LRU by activation frequency). On idle, rotate to cover high-probable experts instead of all experts.
- Result: best cost/latency tradeoff in practice: reduced spike frequency by ~70% while only increasing GPU residency overhead by ~1–2% memory and negligible cost. Complexity: moderate (need to track expert hotness and schedule evictions).

D) Fast-path kernel fusion and reduced kernel launches
- Approach: merge small kernels executed on first token (gating post-processing + expert dispatch) into fused kernels to avoid repeated launches.
- Result: decreased kernel launch overhead by ~40% and shaved ~20—50 ms off first-token in our A100 runs. Complexity: high (backend kernel engineering + correctness testing across model shapes).

E) Prefetch-on-length-threshold
- Approach: detect request with length > threshold and prefetch/allocate larger KV buffers and likely experts asynchronously during routing.
- Result: eliminated the context-scaling cold penalty in >80% of test cases; cost modest (memory overhead during request lifecycle). Works best combined with eager gating.

Comparative notes across architectures

- Llama-MoE: moderate gating compute, large expert weight sizes — memcpy cost dominates. Responds well to prefetch and staggered resident experts.
- Mistral-MoE: lower per-token kernel cost (kernel-fused paths exist), but gating is slightly heavier; eager gating yields bigger wins here.
- Qwen-MoE: gating implementation currently less optimized in runtime; shows highest first-token gating overhead — implementing fused gating+dispatch is prioritized.

Operational recommendations

1) Short term (low-effort, high-impact): implement staggered resident experts + eager gating precompute. These two combined gave >75% reduction in observed P95 spikes in our synthetic bursts without materially increasing billable tokens.
2) Medium term: invest in fused kernels for initial dispatch path and kernel-launch batching for one-off kernels. This is more engineering heavy but removes a recurring root cause.
3) Endpoint-level knobs: expose a per-route "cold-recovery" policy with options: keepwarm-rate, resident-expert-budget, eager-gating (on/off), and prefetch-length-threshold. Allow customers to choose low-cost or low-latency tradeoffs.
4) Telemetry: add fine-grained async traces for first-token paths (memcpy, gating, kernel launch, expert-sync) and link to alerting for rising first-token P95.

Open questions and follow-ups

- How does multi-GPU sharding (expert placement across GPUs) change cold penalties? Our limited 4xH100 test showed similar patterns but with additional inter-GPU sync delays; need larger-scale runs.
- Can we reduce memcpy volume via on-device compression that the runtime can operate on (zero-conversion)? This could shrink rehydrate time for quantized experts.
- Should we expose gating fingerprints so that front-end clients can send a short prefix hint to accelerate routing? Security/abuse considerations need evaluation.

Appendix: quick numeric example (A100 single-GPU)

- Baseline warm per-token: 14 ms
- First-token cold (no mitigation): 220 ms
- First-token with keepwarm: 120 ms
- First-token with eager gating + staggered resident experts: 58 ms
- Context-expansion pause (no mitigation): 130 ms
- Context-expansion with prefetch-on-length-threshold: 18 ms

Action items

- Prototype eager-gating cache in runtime branch (owner: Marcus Liu) — target: proof-of-concept by 2025-10-09.
- Implement slow-path traces for first-token (owner: Priya Menon) — target: 2025-10-02.
- Run full multi-GPU sharded experiments for 8xH100 (owner: Aisha Khan) — target: 2025-10-16.

Notes-to-self

- Watch for interactions with autoscaler: warm policies that keep small allocation alive are effective but must be coordinated with cluster-level cost accounting.
- Communicate findings to solutions-eng for customer-facing guidance (recommended endpoint knobs).

End of note.
